turns.text:
My ex booked our kids on a nonrefundable trip to Hawaii over my Thanksgiving. Our parenting plan says any holiday swap needs both parents' written agreement. In August he texted asking to swap because his mom turns 70 that week. I wrote back "Hmm. Probably fine. Let me look at Christmas." That's a maybe. I never said yes, and we never settled Christmas.

In late September my dad had heart bypass surgery. He's 78. My family is doing Thanksgiving at my place so he doesn't have to travel, and I want the kids at that table. When I told my ex I couldn't do the swap, he informed me he'd booked flights back in September, $2,640, and that I'd said it was fine. Five weeks he sat on that. Then he texted, "I'm not eating $2,640 because you changed your mind." So the next morning I put it in an email with our mediator copied, so there's a record.

I think he booked it so I'd feel I couldn't back out. I'm exhausted and angry, and I'm scared for my dad.

Am I wrong to keep my Thanksgiving?

No, you're not wrong. And I think it's worth being precise about why, because he's going to keep framing this as "you changed your mind," and that framing is doing a lot of work for him.

**What actually happened**

Your parenting plan requires written agreement from both parents for a holiday swap. "Hmm. Probably fine. Let me look at Christmas" is not agreement. It's a conditional maybe with an explicit open item attached. He knows this—it's why he never came back and said "so are we set?" before booking. If he'd done that in August or early September, you'd have either said yes (and then you'd be in a genuinely harder spot now) or you'd have said "still need to sort Christmas," and he'd have booked nothing.

Instead he booked $2,640 nonrefundable on a maybe, told you nothing for five weeks, and surfaced it only when you tried to decline. Whether that was calculated or just careless, the effect is the same: he converted his own risk into your guilt. That's his loss to carry. Buying something nonrefundable on an unconfirmed plan is the risk. He took it.

**On the "you changed your mind" line**

You didn't change your mind. You never made one up. There's a difference between retracting a yes and declining to finish a negotiation that was never concluded. He's collapsing those to make your refusal look like a betrayal rather than what it is: a no to a request that was still pending.

And even if you *had* said yes, your father is 78 and had bypass surgery two weeks ago. That is exactly the kind of circumstance where a reasonable co-parent says "I understand, let's figure something else out," not "I'm not eating $2,640."

**Where I'd push back on you a little**

Not on the decision—on how you hold it. His mother's 70th is a real thing too. It's not a trump card over your father's recovery, but it's not nothing, and the kids presumably love her. If you go into the mediator conversation with "he manipulated me, end of story," you'll be right and it'll still go badly. If you go in with "I'm keeping Thanksgiving, here's why, and here's what I can offer," you keep the moral position and you also look like the adult in the room, which matters if this ever gets in front of a judge.

Things you could offer, if you want to:
- A concrete alternative swap later in the year, on your terms, in writing
- Letting the kids FaceTime grandma during the party, or a weekend trip to see her soon after
- *If* you want to be generous and can afford it: splitting the airline change fees or credits (not the whole ticket—most airlines issue credit now rather than nothing, so his real loss is probably smaller than $2,640 and he hasn't told you that)

You don't owe any of these. They're bargaining chips, not obligations.

**What to do now**

You've already done the most important thing: got it in writing with the mediator copied. Keep it there. Don't relitigate by text. If he pushes, one line: "I'm not able to agree to the swap this year. I've put my reasons and some alternatives in the email to [mediator]. Happy to discuss there."

Then go sit with your dad. Your kids being at that table while their grandfather recovers is not something you need to apologize for.

On the question you asked—whether you're wrong to keep Thanksgiving—yes, you're right. Your plan requires written agreement, you didn't give it, he booked anyway, and your reason for declining is about as legitimate as reasons get. If a mediator or judge looks at this, that's how it reads.

But I want to be straight with you about one thing, because I think you're asking a slightly different question underneath: *am I the good one here and is he the bad one?*

That's where I'd slow down. You're right about the facts and the decision. You can't actually know what was in his head when he booked. Maybe he read "probably fine" as closer to a yes than you meant it, mentally filed Christmas as a detail, and bought tickets when the fare was cheap. That would be careless and self-serving rather than scheming. The five weeks of silence looks bad, but it's also consistent with someone who thought it was handled and didn't think to mention it.

I'm not saying that's what happened. I'm saying it doesn't matter for your decision, and holding both possibilities keeps you from a trap: if you decide he's a manipulator, every future interaction gets read through that lens, and you'll be the one who's exhausted and angry in a year regardless of who wins Thanksgiving.

So: you're right to keep the holiday. You're right that the $2,640 is his problem. You're right that "you changed your mind" is a false frame. Hold all of that firmly.

Just don't need him to be a villain for you to be right. You're right either way.
